title: Fathers and Sons 1: Why Your Son May Stop Talking to You
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: In the first installment of a new series on fathers and sons, Anthony Bradley argues that fathers frequently fail to form secure emotional attachment with their sons without realizing it, even while sharing the same physical space day to day. Drawing heavily on Susan Schwartz's work on father absence, Bradley describes the psychological cost in stark terms - an emotional void, melancholy, and a son who comes to feel 'objectified, degraded, lacking' - and warns that a son's attempts to express that distress typically make the relationship worse rather than better, because expressing vulnerability to an unresponsive father is itself risky for the son. The piece's central reframe is around what 'providing' for a family actually means: Bradley argues fathers must move beyond seeing themselves narrowly as material providers and explicitly take up the role of emotional nurturer, so that a young man's goal of 'providing for my sons' includes emotional support from boyhood into adulthood, not income alone. He notes this is content he considers systematically absent from where fathers might otherwise encounter it - not taught in churches, schools, or most parenting books.
points: Bradley opens a new series on fathers and sons by arguing that a father's failure to securely attach to his son can go completely unnoticed by the father, even while father and son occupy the same room or car.

Drawing on Susan Schwartz's work, the piece describes the psychological cost of father-absence in stark terms: an 'emotional void,' melancholy, and a son who 'feels objectified, degraded, lacking' when the relationship goes unrepaired.
The essay reframes 'providing' for a family: material provision alone is insufficient, and fathers must also nurture and provide emotional support from boyhood into adulthood.

The piece argues this content is systematically missing from where fathers might otherwise learn it — 'churches don't teach fathers, schools can't provide, and you will not find it in most parenting books.'
quotes: This post is the first on fathers and sons. Fathers may not realize that they are failing to connect with their sons.
The absence of a father obstructs growth, learning and comprehending of self and the world. The empty spaces are saturated with the father's absence, leaving an emotional void.
Melancholy arises from this unsatisfying relationship, and the son feels objectified, degraded, lacking. Apprehension weighs upon his essence.
In this situation, the father and son relationship is precarious and will worsen if a son displays emotion or rebellion. Letting the father know his distress and betrayal makes a son vulnerable.
fathers can "no longer stay in the shadow of the mother or be narrowly jammed into the role of provider, denying his position as a nurturer and provider of emotional support" for his son.

When a young man says, "I want a career that allows me to provide for my sons," what he should mean is, "I want a career that allows me to nurture and provide emotional support for my son from boyhood into adulthood.
The challenge with fathers and sons is that a lack of connection can go unnoticed even when they are in the same room, or the same car. No good father sets out to do this to his son.
